# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of the distal coronary vasculature in the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease [1]. First systematically described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the condition was initially regarded as a curiosity but is now recognized as a clinically relevant cause of recurrent chest pain and acute coronary events [2]. Although frequently underdiagnosed, CSFP has important implications for patient quality of life and prognosis [3].

## Definition and Diagnosis

CSFP is most commonly quantified using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (TFC), an objective and reproducible measure introduced by Gibson et al. [4]. A corrected TFC exceeding two standard deviations above the normal range for a given vessel defines slow flow [5]. The TIMI flow grade system, although more qualitative, remains widely used in clinical practice [6]. Accurate measurement requires standardized cine-acquisition rates, and the left anterior descending artery count is conventionally corrected by a factor of 1.7 owing to its greater length [4].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is reported in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [7]. It demonstrates a striking male predominance and frequently occurs in younger smokers presenting with rest angina [8]. The phenomenon accounts for a meaningful proportion of patients presenting with acute coronary syndromes who have angiographically normal or near-normal coronary arteries [9].

## Pathophysiology

The underlying mechanisms of CSFP remain incompletely understood and are likely multifactorial. Microvascular dysfunction is considered central, with elevated microvascular resistance demonstrated by Doppler-derived coronary flow reserve studies [10]. Endothelial dysfunction has been consistently implicated, with reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilatation reported in affected patients [11]. Histopathological examination of myocardial biopsies has revealed small-vessel changes including fibromuscular hyperplasia, endothelial swelling, and luminal narrowing [12].

Subclinical diffuse atherosclerosis has also been proposed, with intravascular ultrasound demonstrating widespread intimal thickening and calcification even in angiographically smooth vessels [13]. Inflammation appears to play a contributory role, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, and other inflammatory markers observed in CSFP cohorts [14]. Increased oxidative stress and impaired antioxidant defenses have similarly been documented [15]. Platelet dysfunction, increased mean platelet volume, and a prothrombotic milieu have been linked to the phenomenon [16]. Metabolic abnormalities, including insulin resistance and components of the metabolic syndrome, are frequently associated [17].

## Clinical Presentation

The dominant symptom is recurrent angina, which may occur at rest and can be refractory to conventional anti-anginal therapy [18]. A substantial proportion of patients experience recurrent hospital admissions and undergo repeated angiography [19]. Beyond stable angina, CSFP has been associated with acute coronary syndromes, ventricular arrhythmias, and, rarely, sudden cardiac death [20]. Documented myocardial ischemia, including transient electrocardiographic changes and perfusion defects on stress imaging, supports its pathological significance [21].

## Associated Electrophysiological Findings

CSFP has been linked to abnormalities of cardiac repolarization, including prolonged QT dispersion and increased Tp-e interval, which may predispose to arrhythmias [22]. Increased P-wave dispersion, signaling an arrhythmogenic atrial substrate, has also been reported in association with atrial fibrillation risk [23].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment algorithm for CSFP, reflecting limited randomized trial data. Dihydropyridine and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, particularly diltiazem, have shown benefit in reducing TFC and improving symptoms [24]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric oxide–potentiating properties, has demonstrated improvement in both angiographic flow and endothelial function [25]. Statins exert pleiotropic effects, improving endothelial function and reducing inflammation, and have been associated with favorable outcomes [26]. Dipyridamole and other agents targeting microvascular resistance have been investigated with variable results [27]. Lifestyle modification, especially smoking cessation, is strongly recommended given the epidemiological associations [28]. Mibefradil and nicorandil have shown promise in small studies but require further evaluation [29].

## Prognosis

Although historically regarded as benign, contemporary data suggest that CSFP carries a non-trivial burden of recurrent symptoms, impaired quality of life, and occasional major adverse cardiovascular events over long-term follow-up [30]. Continued research into standardized diagnostic criteria and evidence-based therapy is warranted.

## Conclusion

CSFP is an increasingly recognized clinical entity with complex pathophysiology centered on microvascular and endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and diffuse atherosclerosis. While generally less ominous than obstructive coronary disease, its impact on symptoms and occasional serious complications justify careful evaluation and individualized management. Larger prospective trials are needed to define optimal therapeutic strategies.
